summary: A mountainous landlocked country in southeastern Central Asia, with the Pamir Plateau covering most of its territory; it is the only country in Central Asia whose main language belongs to the Persian group, and it became independent from the Soviet Union in 1991.

ranking.name: Islam (Sunni)
ranking.description: In the early 8th century the Arab general Qutayba ibn Muslim conquered Central Asia and Islam came with him; in the 9th–10th centuries the Persian Samanid dynasty, with its capital at Bukhara, vigorously promoted Sunnism and Persian culture, and the Tajiks regard it as the source of their national state. From the 1920s the Soviet Union pursued atheism, closing mosques and religious schools, but Islamic customs continued in the home. After independence in 1991 religion revived, and in the 1992–1997 civil war the Islamic Renaissance Party was the main force of the opposition, while after the war the government strictly controlled religious activity.

ranking.name: Islam (Shia Ismaili)
ranking.description: Ismaili believers are mainly the Pamiris of the eastern Gorno-Badakhshan Autonomous Region. In the 11th century the Persian poet and thinker Nasir Khusraw spread Ismaili teachings in the Pamir mountains, and the isolation of the high mountains allowed this faith to survive. Today its followers take the Aga Khan as their spiritual leader, and the Aga Khan Development Network also invests in education and health care there.

ranking.name: Other (Russian Orthodoxy, etc.)
ranking.description: Russian Orthodoxy arrived mainly with the Russians who came with the Russian Empire's conquest of Central Asia in the late 19th century and during the Soviet period. During the 1992–1997 civil war large numbers of Russians and other residents of European descent left Tajikistan, sharply reducing the number of Christians, and now only small communities remain in places such as the capital, Dushanbe.

religion.background: The ancient Tajik region belonged to the Sogdian and Bactrian cultural sphere, where Zoroastrianism and Buddhism once flourished. After the Arab conquest of the 8th century Islam gradually replaced the old faiths, and under the Samanid dynasty Sunnism and Persian culture flourished here. The Pamir mountains became a stronghold of Ismailism after the 11th century. From the 1920s the Soviet Union pursued atheism and religious activity was strictly restricted; religion revived after independence in 1991, but the government still controls religious education, dress and other matters.

language.official: The official language is Tajik, and Russian is the language of interethnic communication.

ranking.name: Tajik
ranking.description: Tajik is a variety of Persian; in the 9th–10th centuries under the Samanid dynasty, poets such as Rudaki, hailed as the "father of Persian poetry," laid the foundation of New Persian literature here, and the Tajiks therefore regard the Persian literary tradition as their own heritage. In 1929 the Soviet Union established the Tajik Soviet Socialist Republic, and the script was changed from the Arabic alphabet to the Latin alphabet and then in 1940 to Cyrillic. In 1989 Tajik became the state language, and since Tajiks make up more than 80 percent of the country, it is the mother tongue of the majority.

ranking.name: Uzbek
ranking.description: Uzbeks live mainly in the northern Sughd Region and in the western areas near Uzbekistan. When the Soviet Union drew the borders of the Central Asian national republics in 1924–1929, it assigned the Tajik-speaking cities of Samarkand and Bukhara to Uzbekistan and also placed many Uzbek-populated areas inside Tajikistan; the two peoples live interspersed in the Fergana Valley, so Uzbek is the second-largest language.

ranking.name: Russian
ranking.description: Russian was the language of administration, science and interethnic communication in the Tsarist and Soviet periods. After the civil war of the 1990s large numbers of Russians left and the number of native Russian speakers fell sharply, but the constitution still designates it the "language of interethnic communication." Because millions of Tajiks go to work in Russia, Russian remains an important second language today.

ranking.name: Kyrgyz
ranking.description: Kyrgyz speakers are mainly the Kyrgyz of the Murghab region of the eastern Pamir Plateau and of the Jirgatol area in the north, who traditionally live as nomadic herders of yaks and sheep. These areas border Kyrgyzstan and were assigned to Tajikistan when the Soviet Union drew the borders, thus forming minority communities.

language.history: Tajik belongs to the Iranian branch of the Indo-European family and is the Central Asian variety of Persian, mutually intelligible with the Persian of Iran and the Dari of Afghanistan. In ancient times Sogdian and Bactrian were in common use there, and after Islamization in the 8th century New Persian arose under the Samanid dynasty and replaced the old languages. In the Soviet period Tajik was changed first to the Latin and then to the Cyrillic alphabet, parting ways in writing from the Persian of Iran, which uses the Arabic script. The Pamir mountains still preserve several Eastern Iranian Pamir languages, such as Shughni and Wakhi.

ranking.name: Tajik plov (osh)
ranking.description: Lamb and onions are first fried until fragrant in a large iron cauldron, then a large amount of yellow carrot strips and rice are added and slowly steamed in mutton fat into pilaf, often with chickpeas, raisins or garlic added.
ranking.history: Plov is a traditional dish along the Silk Road in Central Asia; similar rice dishes are recorded in the works of the medieval physician Ibn Sina (Avicenna), and popular legend even says it originated with the army of Alexander the Great. In Tajikistan plov is the core dish of weddings, funerals, welcoming guests and religious holidays, and is traditionally cooked outdoors in a large cauldron by male cooks for hundreds of people to share. In 2016 "Oshi palav, a traditional meal in Tajikistan" was added to UNESCO's Intangible Cultural Heritage list.

ranking.name: Kurutob (yogurt and bread salad)
ranking.description: Dried salty yogurt balls called "qurut" are dissolved in water and poured over torn layered flatbread, which is then topped with onion, tomato, cucumber and herbs and eaten by hand from a wooden platter.
ranking.history: Qurut is a way that nomadic and mountain peoples of Central Asia preserve milk: yogurt is salted, rolled into small balls and dried, so that it can be kept for months, suitable for long migrations and for winter. Kurutob is regarded as the national dish of Tajikistan and is traditionally eaten by the whole family or guests sitting around and sharing from the same large wooden platter by hand, symbolizing sharing and hospitality. It is also very common in the traditional teahouses of Dushanbe.

ranking.name: Sambusa (baked pastry)
ranking.description: Layered dough is filled with diced lamb, mutton fat and onion, shaped into a triangle or square, and baked stuck to the inner wall of a tandoor (clay oven), crisp outside and juicy inside.
ranking.history: This filled pastry is called "sanbosag" in Persian, and the 11th-century Persian historian Bayhaqi already mentions it; it spread with Silk Road travelers to the Middle East, South Asia and East Africa and evolved into triangular fried pastries in different places. In Central Asia, like bread, it is baked in a round clay oven rather than fried, which shows the local food culture centered on the tandoor. Today it is the most common snack in Tajik markets and teahouses.

ranking.name: Shashlik (grilled skewers)
ranking.description: Pieces of lamb, beef or chicken are marinated and threaded onto iron skewers, grilled over charcoal until charred outside and tender inside, and eaten with raw onion and flatbread.
ranking.history: The tradition of charcoal-grilled skewers among the nomadic peoples of Central Asia is a long one, and the name "shashlik" comes from Crimean Tatar and spread through Russian, becoming in the Soviet period the common name throughout the Soviet region. In Tajikistan skewers are a common food in teahouses, markets and weekend family gatherings, often enjoyed with green tea, flatbread and salad.

ranking.name: Shurbo (lamb soup)
ranking.description: A clear broth made from lamb, slowly stewed with potato, carrot, onion, tomato and chickpeas and sprinkled with cilantro, with a clean, sweet, rich broth.
ranking.history: The word "shurbo" derives from Persian and belongs to the same family as the "shorba" soups of Central Asia and the Middle East, reflecting the influence of Persian culture on local food. The potato reached Central Asia in the late 19th century with the expansion of the Russian Empire, which gave this soup its present form. In the cold mountain winters, lamb soup is the most common warming staple of Tajik families and is also often used to entertain guests.
